item.text:
Below is a text-only review of the supplied amendment, not verification of the bill’s official text or status. Some items are clear gaps; others are potential interpretations or challenges whose success would depend on regulations, existing law, and courts. An omitted enforcement provision does not necessarily mean the government lacks that power under other law.

### Coverage and definitions

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—A strict threshold, not an inclusive one.** A model trained using exactly \(10^{26}\) operations falls outside this prong because the text requires “greater than” that amount. Models below or at the threshold remain potentially covered by a capability determination under § 2(1)(B).

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Single training run” is undefined and not aggregated.** Companies could argue that pretraining, subsequent training, fine-tuning, or separately scheduled stages are distinct runs, each below the threshold. The bill supplies no rule for combining related runs or preventing artificial segmentation.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Separate models can form a more capable system.** An ensemble, network of agents, or system combining several smaller models might exceed the intended capability level without any individual model crossing the training threshold. Such systems would depend on § 2(1)(B) for coverage.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** “Computing power” ordinarily describes a rate or capacity, but the definition uses a cumulative operation count; it also leaves actual versus estimated operations, numerical precision, and specialized hardware treatment unspecified. Different accounting methods could place the same training project on opposite sides of the threshold.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Training compute is an imperfect proxy for capability.** More efficient algorithms, knowledge transferred from larger models, or substantial computation during use could produce highly capable systems below the training threshold. Conversely, the threshold could capture expensive but comparatively limited models; these are scope and calibration problems, not automatic legal defects.

6. **§§ 2(1), 3(a)—Unclear when a project becomes covered.** Prong (A) describes a model already “trained” above the threshold, while § 3 prohibits training it. The text does not clearly establish whether beginning an intended above-threshold run is prohibited, or whether liability starts only when the threshold is crossed.

7. **§ 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never defines which Secretary makes capability determinations. Commerce’s registry role suggests one interpretation, but the express reference to the Secretary of State elsewhere makes this an avoidable allocation-of-authority problem.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—The capability standard is indeterminate.** “Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks” supplies no task universe, weighting method, human comparison group, or testing conditions. Coverage could change substantially depending on whether the comparison is to an average individual, trained specialists, or humans using tools.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Coverage appears to require an affirmative determination.** A highly capable system below the compute threshold arguably remains outside the definition until the Secretary acts. There is no deadline, mandatory assessment process, or requirement that developers submit potentially qualifying systems for review.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure or rules for changed systems.** The bill does not specify notice, evidence, testing access, publication, when a determination takes effect, or whether it covers subsequent versions and derivatives. Ordinary administrative-law procedures and judicial review may apply, but the text leaves important questions unresolved.

11. **§§ 2(1)(B), 5—Vagueness and delegation challenges.** An open-ended capability standard backed by substantial civil penalties and imprisonment invites fair-notice challenges and potentially a challenge to the breadth of delegated authority. Those challenges would not automatically succeed, and criminal willfulness offers some protection, but neither issue is clearly resolved by the drafting.

12. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—“U.S. person” excludes several categories of people.** The definition omits lawful permanent residents and noncitizen U.S. nationals. Those individuals are covered while in the United States, but their activities abroad are not expressly reached merely because of their U.S. residence or ties.

13. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—“U.S. person” excludes numerous business forms.** LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other noncorporate entities are not expressly included, and corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law are not clearly covered by “laws of a State.” This creates potential gaps in the overseas prohibition, although covered individuals involved could still face liability.

14. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not expressly attributed to U.S. parents.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary operating abroad is not itself a “U.S. person” under this definition. The bill contains no ownership, control, or attribution rule automatically treating its conduct as the U.S. parent’s, though the parent’s own participation could still matter.

15. **§ 3(a)—The location of distributed activity is unclear.** The bill does not explain how to locate training or deployment when personnel, servers, corporate operators, and customers are in different countries. Whether foreign-hosted services offered to U.S. users constitute prohibited activity “in the United States” could become a significant dispute.

### Prohibition and exceptions

16. **§ 3(a)—“Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” are undefined.** It is unclear whether these terms include fine-tuning, integrating a model into another product, publishing model weights, providing API access, or continuing to operate an already deployed service. “Develop” is especially broad and could generate both expansive enforcement claims and fair-notice objections.

17. **§ 3(a)—Possession, transfers, and ordinary use are not expressly prohibited.** The text does not separately ban acquiring, importing, selling, transferring, possessing, or using a covered system. Some conduct might count as development or deployment, but the text does not ensure that all such activities are covered.

18. **§ 3(a)—No tailored rule for intermediaries or assistance.** Cloud providers, chip suppliers, financiers, and other intermediaries are not expressly liable merely for facilitating prohibited work. Generally applicable criminal aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy law may reach qualifying conduct, but the bill supplies no specific civil facilitation rule or intermediary compliance duty.

19. **§§ 2(1), 3(a)—Potential reach into protected research and publication.** A broad reading of “develop” or “deploy” could encompass publishing code or research rather than merely operating dangerous systems. Applications involving protected expression could face First Amendment challenges, although not all AI development or deployment is protected speech.

20. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts entire systems, not just unfinished training.** The exception says subsection (a) does not apply to a qualifying existing system at all. On its face, that permits continued training, development, and deployment—not merely completion of a run already underway.

21. **§ 3(b)—“Training began” has no minimum or documentation requirement.** A developer could argue that a small preliminary training step before enactment preserves the exemption for a much larger future project. The bill requires neither substantial progress nor a contemporaneous filing establishing the start date.

22. **§ 3(b)—No boundary between an existing system and a new one.** The text does not address new versions, substantial retraining, derivatives, merged models, or systems built around grandfathered components. Developers could characterize later projects as continuations of exempt systems, and transfer of an exempt system is not expressly restricted.

23. **§ 3(c)—Safety evaluation is an unrestricted purpose-based exception.** There is no definition, approved evaluator requirement, advance authorization, containment standard, or limit on scale or duration. Training, development, and deployment could all be claimed as exempt when conducted for safety evaluation.

24. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose and downstream activities are unresolved.** The exception does not require safety evaluation to be the sole or primary purpose, leaving room for activities that also advance commercial development. Nor does it expressly regulate retention or transfer of resulting models, although later activities would still need their own exemption if otherwise prohibited.

25. **§§ 3(b)–(c), 5—Exception procedures and proof are unspecified.** There is no required recordkeeping to support grandfathering or safety-evaluation claims, and the bill does not allocate the burden of establishing those exceptions. Default procedural rules may govern, but proving or rebutting a claimed exception could be difficult.

### Registry and oversight

26. **§ 2(3)—“Advanced AI chips” is undefined.** The bill supplies no performance standard, technical specification, or updating mechanism. Operators could dispute whether particular accelerators or alternative hardware count toward the facility threshold.

27. **§§ 2(3), 4—Facility size is disconnected from prohibited activity.** A facility with exactly 50,000 qualifying chips need not register, and smaller facilities may still train covered systems over time or participate in distributed training. Conversely, a large facility must register regardless of whether it handles any covered system.

28. **§§ 2(3), 4—No aggregation or facility-boundary rule.** “Data center” does not explain whether adjoining buildings, separately operated halls, or interconnected sites constitute one facility. Physically dividing infrastructure could avoid registration without avoiding the underlying § 3 prohibition.

29. **§ 4—The responsible operator and geographic reach are unclear.** The text does not allocate duties among owners, colocation providers, cloud operators, and tenants, or specify whether overseas facilities are included. Unlike § 3, the registry provision has no express territorial or U.S.-person limitation.

30. **§ 4(a)–(b)—Registration and reporting deadlines are incomplete.** There is no initial registration deadline, quarterly filing date, reporting calendar, or rule for facilities crossing the threshold. Reporting applies to “registered” operators, creating an additional textual argument about report liability for an operator that never registered, even though nonregistration would breach subsection (a).

31. **§ 4(b)—Reports need not contain the information required to enforce § 3.** “Describing the computing workloads” does not expressly require per-run operation counts, model identities, training start dates, customers, distributed-training links, or exemption claims. Operator certification is not independent verification, and quarterly reporting could reveal activity only after substantial work is complete.

32. **§§ 2(1)(B), 4—No express investigative or technical-access powers.** The bill does not grant inspection, audit, subpoena, testing-access, or record-retention authority. Existing powers may help, but the text supplies no dedicated mechanism for verifying compute use or evaluating systems whose operators withhold access.

33. **§§ 4, 5—No express penalty for registry violations.** Both penalty provisions apply only to violations of § 3, not failures to register or report under § 4. Knowingly false submissions may trigger other federal laws, but those laws do not automatically provide a complete remedy for missing or inadequate reports.

### Penalties and implementation

34. **§ 5(a)—The civil enforcement process is unspecified.** The bill does not identify who assesses or seeks civil penalties, whether proceedings are administrative or judicial, or what hearing and collection procedures apply. General law may fill portions of the gap, but “shall be liable” is not a complete enforcement framework.

35. **§§ 3, 5—No express mechanism to halt ongoing work or dispose of systems.** The bill specifies fines and imprisonment but no dedicated stop-work orders, emergency injunction authority, equipment seizure, or model-disposition remedy. Courts or agencies may have other applicable authority, but the bill itself does not establish those tools.

36. **§ 5(a)—The daily penalty unit is ambiguous.** It is unclear whether the $1 million ceiling applies per person per day, per system per day, or separately to training, development, and deployment violations. The text also does not say when a completed act becomes a continuing violation, potentially producing very different penalty totals.

37. **§ 5(b)—Willfulness may be difficult to prove.** Criminal cases would require proof of a willful violation against a backdrop of uncertain coverage and broad exceptions. The precise knowledge requirement would depend on judicial interpretation, and a corporate conviction cannot itself imprison responsible individuals without establishing their personal criminal liability.

38. **§§ 5(a), 8—Enactment-date penalties conflict with delayed effectiveness.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act’s effect for 180 days. The stronger reading is that conduct cannot violate a prohibition not yet effective, but the mismatch invites disputes and fair-notice objections.

39. **§§ 3(b), 8—The implementation window and grandfathering cutoff differ.** Training started after enactment but before day 180 would apparently be lawful initially yet ineligible for grandfathering. The text does not explain the status of systems completed or deployed during that window, particularly whether leaving an existing deployment running is a new or continuing violation.

40. **§§ 2–5, 8—No express rulemaking authority or implementation timetable.** The bill leaves substantial technical and procedural details unresolved without expressly authorizing implementing regulations or requiring them before enforcement begins. Implied or existing authority may be available, but it should not be assumed to resolve every gap before day 180.

### International agreement and duration

41. **§ 6—Negotiation is required, not an agreement or foreign compliance.** “Seek to negotiate” does not ensure that another country accepts equivalent restrictions, and the 18-month language is unclear about whether negotiations must begin or reach some milestone. The provision neither directly binds foreign actors nor specifies verification, enforcement, or consequences if negotiations fail.

42. **§ 7(a)—The National Academies report has no commissioning mechanism.** The bill relies on a report without requiring anyone to request it, funding it, setting a deadline, or specifying its scope. That could leave the early-termination process without the report Congress is supposed to act on.

43. **§ 7(a)—The safety finding and termination mechanism are underspecified.** “Can be developed safely” does not define acceptable risk or explain whether safety must be shown for all covered systems or only certain classes and conditions. The text appears to provide a single termination trigger for the entire prohibition, and a joint resolution changing legal obligations ordinarily must satisfy presentment requirements—not merely secure congressional approval.

44. **§ 7(a)–(b)—The sunset ends the prohibition regardless of safety.** Although subsection (a) says the prohibition remains until a congressional safety finding, subsection (b) ends the entire Act after ten years even without that finding. Conversely, if Congress ends the prohibition earlier, the registry appears to remain operative until the sunset because subsection (a) terminates only § 3’s prohibition.

45. **§ 7(b)—No transition rules for expiration.** The bill does not specify treatment of final reports, records, outstanding orders, or ongoing proceedings when the Act ceases to have effect. The general federal saving statute may preserve incurred liabilities and penalties, so expiration should not be described as automatically erasing past violations.
